chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
title: Italian dancers, and the first Black band in a white hall on Pine Street
summary: White Italian youths from Dago Hill began coming to the Black dance hall and then hired Creath for a white hall on Pine Street, a first for a Black band in segregated St. Louis.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: And then this was a colored dance hall, but these Italian boys and all around St. Louis started to hear about this jazz and they started to come into this dance hall 'cause they could dance by this music. And boy, we had as many white as blacks. They almost took it over because they loved that music. And Charlie was reading about jazz, jazz, jazz, you know, they called it jazz o'maniacs. That was the name -- and we rehearsed every week, once a week, and from then on why the Italian boys started to want to hire Charlie for their dances.
And did they -- up from Dago Hill.

From Dago Hill. And they wanted -- and there was the first white place we played was a hall on Pine Street -- I've forgotten the name of it but that was -- these Italian boys, some of their friends owned this band so they got them to hire Charlie's band 'cause they'd had always white bands.

No, no, the Arcadian was like Roselord, and we were the first black band to play. They got Charlie to play at this hall on Pine Street. That's where it was -- in those days it was segregation, it wasn't integrated. It was all white at this dance hall, and that's where Jack Bland and --
